channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Scientists breed a 'pan-African' malaria parasite to build a better whole-parasite malaria vaccine
item.description: Researchers have created a hybrid malaria parasite that combines the manufacturing advantages of the strain used in every current whole-parasite malaria vaccine with the much higher liver infectivity of a parasite collected recently in East Africa. The work is published in JCI Insight.

item.title: Q&A: Rethinking immunity beyond 'strong' and 'weak'
item.description: Melinda Fagan, professor in the Department of Philosophy at the University of Utah, where she holds the Sterling M. McMurrin Chair, proposed in a recent paper a new approach to understanding immunity for both experts and nonexperts, which could help address vaccine hesitancy in a science-leery public.

item.title: Waves that clear waste from the brain during sleep are impaired in older adults
item.description: As people age, they may sleep for shorter periods and wake up more frequently during the night. In addition to those disruptions, MIT researchers have now discovered that a process responsible for flushing waste from the brain during sleep is commonly impaired in older people.

item.title: Hamster hibernation study offers clues to Alzheimer's disease
item.description: Researchers at VIB and KU Leuven have discovered that hibernation triggers changes in brain cells that partially resemble those in Alzheimer's disease. Studying golden hamsters, the team identified changes in gene expression across the hibernation cycle, which resemble those associated with the accumulation of amyloid plaques in Alzheimer's.

item.title: Vitamin D may help control lung inflammation during flu infection, study in mice suggests
item.description: Vitamin D may help the body fight influenza by controlling inflammation and the amount of virus in the lungs, according to a study in mice led by researchers at Penn State.

item.title: AI analysis of heart ultrasounds may help flag long-term cardiovascular or dementia-related death risk
item.description: Having a heart age older than one's actual age, as estimated using artificial intelligence (AI) analysis of ultrasound images, was associated with worse outcomes, according to results presented today at the ESC Digital & AI Summit 2026.

item.title: Human-to-human hantavirus spread confirmed on cruise ship
item.description: In April 2026, an outbreak of severe respiratory infections, presenting as hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), was detected aboard the cruise ship M/V Hondius, which had left Ushuaia, Argentina, on April 1. Analyses conducted by the UNIGE/HUG Geneva Center for Emerging Viral Diseases, a WHO Collaborating Center, identified the virus as belonging to the Andes strain. In total, 13 passengers were affected, three of whom died.

item.title: Does a heart stent prevent future heart attacks in stable patients? 25-year follow-up offers new insight
item.description: When doctors find a blockage in a patient's heart arteries, a common treatment option is a procedure to open the artery and restore blood flow. But does getting a stent actually help prevent a future heart attack or help someone live longer?

item.title: Most new parents have intrusive thoughts about their baby being harmed: It's OK to talk about it
item.description: Telling your friends and family you're pregnant will earn you an avalanche of advice. Yet few parents will ever be told about a common experience that can impact the parents' long-term mental health: perinatal intrusive thoughts.

item.title: Why exercise has become a key part of cancer treatment
item.description: Scientists have long known that regular exercise decreases the risk of developing many types of cancer. But last year, results from a large, randomized clinical trial of patients with colon cancer definitively showed what many observational studies and animal research had been hinting at for decades: People who exercise following cancer treatment have a better chance of surviving the disease and a lower likelihood of recurrence.

item.title: Women's health research highlights the role of molecular testing in precision medicine
item.description: Molecular diagnostic approaches are expanding what information is available for clinicians and laboratory professionals, including uncovering antimicrobial resistance, identifying pathogens missed by conventional methods, revealing cancer recurrence risks and characterizing complex tumor biology.

item.title: GPs are now 'prescribing' time in nature. Is it likely to improve your health?
item.description: Imagine visiting your primary care doctor for your physical or mental health and leaving with a prescription to spend more time outdoors.

item.title: Label-free imaging tracks lipid storage in living liver organoids
item.description: Fat accumulation in liver cells is central to several metabolic disorders, but observing the process in living tissue models remains difficult. Fluorescent labels and stains can provide detailed images, but they may disrupt cells or capture only selected time points. A label-free approach for tracking changes in lipid storage over time in three-dimensional mouse liver organoids is reported in Biophotonics Discovery.

item.title: Sustained clinical responses seen with neuroimmune modulation for rheumatoid arthritis
item.description: Twenty-four-month data show sustained clinical responses for patients receiving neuroimmune modulation therapy for rheumatoid arthritis (RA), according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the American College of Rheumatology, held from Nov. 6 to 11 in Orlando, Florida.

item.title: Stomach cancer is changing: An expert explains surgical approaches
item.description: Sometimes innovation in cancer care means developing something entirely new. Other times, it means returning to an old idea with the knowledge and tools to make it work better. Both are happening in stomach cancer surgery, says Travis Grotz, M.D., a Mayo Clinic surgical oncologist who specializes in treating stomach cancer.

item.title: How the brain rapidly learns to interpret ambiguous images
item.description: Both humans and image recognition algorithms can take time to identify the objects and scenes depicted in some images. Emblematic examples of this phenomenon are Mooney images, pictures that are intentionally reduced to patches of black and white, with no shades of gray.

item.title: Despite programs for firefighter health, most rural firefighters are left behind
item.description: In recent years, several organizations have recognized the firefighting profession's unique and substantial work-related health hazards, including cancers, heart disease, chronic respiratory illnesses and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

item.title: Mobile app and telemonitoring improve quality of life and symptoms in patients with heart failure
item.description: A telemedicine-based management program was well accepted among patients with heart failure and improved their quality of life and self-care, according to results presented today at ESC Digital & AI Summit 2026.

item.title: Taking a closer look at stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation
item.description: Patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), one of the most common heart rhythm disorders, are at increased risk of ischemic stroke, a stroke caused by a blood clot blocking blood flow to the brain, as well as blood clots that can travel to other parts of the body.

item.title: New test identifies people at higher risk of glaucoma, the leading cause of irreversible blindness
item.description: A new genetic test developed by researchers at QIMR Berghofer and Flinders University, along with international collaborators, can identify people at up to 10 times the normal risk of developing open-angle glaucoma, the most common form of the disease and the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide.

item.title: China approves first oral GLP-1 weight-loss pill
item.description: China has approved its first orally administered GLP-1 weight-loss drug, permitting Eli Lilly to sell its orforglipron pill in a market where 630 million adults could be overweight or obese by 2050.

item.title: What men need to know after a major update to prostate cancer guidelines
item.description: Middle-aged men should undergo regular screening for prostate cancer, the American Cancer Society said Thursday in a major change to its guidelines.

item.title: The US and Mexico are on the verge of forfeiting a major health victory. Here's what to know
item.description: International health experts are meeting this week to determine if the United States and Mexico have forfeited one of their greatest public health victories—the elimination of measles.

item.title: Machine-learning models accurately predict mortality after a heart attack
item.description: Machine-learning models were able to predict mortality in the hospital and in the six months after a type of heart attack, according to results presented today at ESC Digital & AI Summit 2026.

item.title: What is 'food is medicine'? Two experts explain this decades‑old approach to health care that is taking on new life
item.description: Mountains of scientific evidence support both the negative and positive effects of our eating habits on our health. Research shows that a healthy diet can help those suffering from chronic health conditions like type 2 diabetes, heart disease and high blood pressure.

item.title: Cervical cancer elimination is in reach—we just need more GP appointments
item.description: For most Australians, general practice (GP) clinics are the first point of contact when seeking medical care. But many of us can relate to the difficulties of booking, paying for and attending an appointment.

item.title: Broad genomic testing linked to longer survival in advanced lung cancer, according to new study
item.description: New research in the November 2026 issue of Journal of the National Comprehensive Cancer Network found that patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) lived longer when they received broad-based genomic sequencing (BGS)—testing a large panel of dozens or hundreds of genes at once—before starting treatment, compared with patients who received more limited biomarker testing of just one or two genes.

item.title: Perceiving greater discrimination in health care, the LGBTQIA+ community delays seeking medical appointments
item.description: People in the LGBTQ+ community face extra barriers in their daily lives due to their sexual orientation or gender identity. One of the areas where these individuals sometimes suffer discrimination is in health care. In fact, a survey by the State Federation of Lesbians, Gays, Trans, Bisexual, and Intersex People found that more than 20% of the trans people surveyed had felt discriminated against when visiting primary care providers.

item.title: Young Australians are paying the price for a health system that doesn't fit their lives
item.description: Gen Z Australians are increasingly delaying health care, missing work and study, or sometimes going without care because of cost, inconvenience and difficulty accessing a general practitioner (GP). Nearly one in three have taken time off work, study or caregiving responsibilities to see a GP, while one in five delayed care because of cost in the past 12 months.

item.title: Infant mortality falls by 16% in some of England's most deprived areas, new national data show
item.description: Infant mortality in some of England's most disadvantaged areas fell by 16% from April 2025 to March 2026 compared with the previous year, according to the latest national data published by the National Child Mortality Database (NCMD) at the University of Bristol.
